problem: The lead says the arc itself is at 1500–2500 °C. That range is the melting range of the metal (steel melts near 1500 °C), not the arc temperature. An arc column is several thousand degrees hot, so a student learns a badly wrong number in the first sentence.
fix: An electric arc hotter than about 6000 °C melts metal whose melting point is 1500–2500 °C. Air would oxidise that molten metal, so each process shields it differently.

where: Section 1 and Quiz Q1 (fourth digit of E6013)
problem: Saying E6013 runs on 'AC or DCEP' only is incomplete. The high-titania potassium (rutile) coating of E6013 also runs on DCEN, and a student may mark DCEN as wrong in an exam.
fix: Fourth digit 3: rutile (high-titania potassium) coating, runs on AC or DC either polarity (DCEP or DCEN).

problem: The 4800 kJ is heat input after multiplying by arc efficiency 0.8, so it is the net heat delivered to the joint. Total arc energy from the arc is V×I/v × length = 6000 kJ. Labelling 4800 kJ 'arc energy' mixes the two terms.
fix: Step 5: Net heat into the joint = H × length = 0.8 kJ/mm × 6000 mm = 4800 kJ (the arc itself delivers 1 kJ/mm × 6000 mm = 6000 kJ; 0.8 of that enters the work). Answer: heat input is 800 J/mm and the joint receives 4800 kJ of net heat.
